I cannot tell what beauty is her dole, Who cannot see her features for her soul. As birds see not the casement for the sky.

But there is another sense in which beauty is the most matter-of-fact thing. I can conceive that if the human family had developed only one eye, and that planted in the centre of the forehead, the appearance of a person with two eyes would be as offensive to our sense of beauty as a hand that consisted not of fingers but of thumbs. We should go to the show to see the two-eyed man with just the same feelings as we go now to see the bearded woman. We should not go to admire his two eyes, any more than we go to admire the beard; we should go to enjoy a pleasant sense of disgust at his misfortune and a comfortable satisfaction at the fact that we had not been the victims of such a calamity. We should roll our single eye with a proud feeling that we were in the true line of beauty, from which the two-eyed man in front was a hideous and fantastic departure.

Beauty, in short, is only a tribute which we pay to necessity. In equipping itself for the struggle for existence humanity has found that it is convenient to have two eyes and a stereoscopic vision, just as it is convenient to have four fingers on the hand and one thumb instead of five thumbs. Our members have been developed in the manner best fitted to enable us to fight our battle. And the more perfectly they fulfil that supreme condition the more beautiful we declare them to be. Our ideas of beauty, therefore, are not absolute; they are conditional. They are the humble servants of our necessity. Two eyes are necessary for us to get about our business, and so we fall in love with two eyes, and the more perfect they are for their work the more we fall in love with them, and the more beautiful we declare them to be.

I think that Peggy, nursing her one-eyed cat there in the sun, has not yet accepted our creed of beauty. She will be as conventional as the rest of us when her frocks are longer.

message.content:
"I find it difficult to define what beauty signifies to her, as one cannot perceive her features beyond her essence. It's akin to how birds overlook the window frame when they gaze at the vast sky.

Nonetheless, beauty can also be viewed from a starkly pragmatic perspective. Imagine if humanity had evolved with a single eye, positioned centrally on the forehead; individuals with two eyes might be regarded as grotesque, much like a hand composed solely of thumbs. We would attend exhibitions featuring the two-eyed individual with the same mindset that we currently have when observing a bearded woman. Our interest would not stem from admiration for his dual vision, just as we do not admire the beard; rather, we would be drawn by a curious sense of disgust at his peculiar condition and a reassuring relief that we had escaped such a plight. We would behold our solitary eye with a sense of pride, convinced we embodied the true standard of beauty, while viewing the two-eyed figure before us as a bizarre deviation from the norm.

Ultimately, beauty serves as a tribute to our practical needs. In the struggle for survival, humanity has found it advantageous to possess two eyes for depth perception, just as having four fingers and one thumb proves more functional than having five thumbs. Our anatomical features have evolved in ways that best equip us for the challenges we face. The more effectively they serve this fundamental purpose, the more we ascribe beauty to them. Consequently, our perceptions of beauty are not absolute but rather dependent on context. The necessity of two eyes enhances our ability to navigate the world, leading us to cherish them even more, with our affection growing in relation to their functional perfection.

I observe that Peggy, cradling her one-eyed cat in the sunlight, has yet to embrace our conventional standards of beauty. However, she will likely conform to these norms as her dresses grow longer."
